newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil govt sees 2.9 pct '96 current account gap.
newsitem.headline: Brazil govt sees 2.9 pct '96 current account gap.

text.p: The Brazilian government expects 1996 to end with a current account gap of 2.9 percent of gross domestic product, presidential spokesman Sergio Amaral said.
Amaral told reporters Finance Minister Pedro Malan had put Brazil's current account deficit for 1996 at 2.9 percent of GDP during a special cabinet meeting Saturday.

Malan, comparing this figure with other countries such as Canada, with a 3.0-4.0 percent current account gap, Australia with 4.0-5.0 percent and Malaysia with a deficit of 6.8 percent of GDP, said it was low.
Amaral said an estimated $8.0 billion in net direct foreign investment this year would cover almost 40 percent of the current account deficit, seen at $20 billion.
"This shows that the most important thing is not the trade deficit, which is not desired and is being countered, but that the current account gap is perfectly manageable," Amaral said.
Amaral also said Saturday's cabinet meeting was told that direct foreign investment in 1997 would be between $10 billion and $12 billion.
"So almost 40 percent of the current account gap will be financed by foreign direct investment, which is healthy," Amaral said.
He added that Brasilia had taken steps to raise exports and would continue to take steps like a package of export-boosting measures announced Friday.
The markets have been nervous about Brazil's trade performance since it posted a record $1.3 billion deficit in October, well above all expectations.
Finance Minister Pedro Malan said Friday November's trade gap would be narrower than October's.
